articles.author: MIT.nano
articles.title: Building connections across the research infrastructure
articles.excerpt: MIT.nano and the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition gathered facility leaders and technology professionals from across the nation to explore ways to make shared-access facilities more connected.
articles.content:
MIT.nano · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

MIT.nano and the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition gathered facility leaders and technology professionals from across the nation to explore ways to make shared-access facilities more connected.

Running a modern research laboratory requires more than maintaining sophisticated instruments. Researchers need to complete training, obtain access, schedule and operate equipment, navigate billing, and more. For large, shared facilities, coordinating these activities across hundreds of instruments and thousands of users can be a significant undertaking. As research becomes increasingly interdisciplinary, another challenge is emerging: finding the right capability in the first place.

Addressing these challenges was a central theme of the 2026 NEMO User Meeting, hosted by MIT.nano Oct. 5–6. The meeting brought together 65 representatives from 25 laboratories and organizations, including facility directors, laboratory managers, technical staff, software developers, industry representatives, and government researchers. Sponsored by the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition (NEMC) hub, the meeting focused on sharing approaches to lab management and building connections among facilities.

At the center of the meeting was the NanoFab Equipment Management and Operations (NEMO) system, an open-source platform that provides tools for managing shared research facilities while allowing individual laboratories to adapt the system to their own needs. The meeting highlighted an important characteristic of the NEMO community: The same platform can serve a very diverse set of facilities, and while the scale or the scientific missions of the facilities may differ, their core operational challenges are often remarkably similar. 

For Anna Osherov, associate director of Characterization.nano and organizer of the meeting, the collaborative model is one of the most compelling aspects of NEMO.

“Open source changes the way we think about technology development,” she says. “We can build on what others have already developed, contribute improvements back to the community, and collectively create a platform that is more capable than what any one facility could develop on its own.”

NEMO was originally released as open-source software by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2018. Its community edition (NEMO-CE), launched in 2023, allows facilities to develop and share extensions to the platform. At the October meeting, participants from organizations including MIT; Stanford, Columbia, and Princeton universities; the University of Pennsylvania; NIST; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; and Atlantis Labs presented tools to address challenges ranging from chemical management and user administration to equipment status, training, and workflow automation.

The range of presentations illustrated how differently configured facilities are adapting a common platform to their own needs. Stanford, for example, presented real-time displays for equipment status and reservations, while Columbia shared its experience migrating to NEMO and extending the system for billing and facility workflows. Princeton demonstrated automated process charts for monitoring tool performance, and the University of Pennsylvania presented approaches to chemical management.

Overall, the projects demonstrated the premise behind the NEMO community: a solution developed to address a problem at one facility can become a resource for others.

“Together we can do way more than any one of us individually can,” said Vladimir Bulović, director of MIT.nano, during his opening remarks. “NEMO is the platform that gave us, finally, a streamlined way to do so.”

From individual facilities to a connected research ecosystem

As the NEMO community grows, another opportunity emerges. Universities and research organizations operate specialized facilities, each with unique equipment, expertise, and capabilities. But researchers cannot use a capability they are unaware of or cannot easily find.

This is particularly important for microelectronics R&D, where progress often depends on moving quickly between specialized capabilities. A researcher may need fabrication at one facility, advanced characterization at another, specialized microscopy somewhere else, and a process or analysis capability available at only a handful of institutions.

Finding those capabilities, and knowing where and when they can be accessed, can itself become a bottleneck.Traditionally, networks of facilities have relied on static webpages or databases to describe available resources. But as facilities evolve, this information can quickly become outdated.

At the meeting, MIT.nano presented Hydra, a new open-source platform being developed with support from NEMC as a key component of the NEMC Technical Concierge, a program that aims to help researchers identify and access specialized capabilities across a network of facilities. Hydra is designed to connect multiple NEMO installations and draw information directly from the systems that facilities already use, rather than requiring someone to manually update a separate database. The result is a compilation built from the ground truths of actively-used facility management systems. “Hydra does not replace any lab management system,” Osherov explained. “It connects, synchronizes, and keeps data up to date across all connected systems in real time.”

In this model, NEMO provides the operational source of information within an individual facility, while Hydra makes that information discoverable across facilities.

For a researcher, that could mean finding a specialized capability without first needing to know which laboratory might have the relevant equipment. 

“The focus is to make the distributed infrastructure supporting research more discoverable and usable,” Osherov said.

Building infrastructure that can change

The approach reflects a broader philosophy: Research infrastructure needs to evolve as research itself changes. “We need to build a flexible research space and a community-oriented space so that people feel empowered to go to it, use it, and then redefine it as the years progress, adapting it to the needs of the next generation of researchers,” said Bulović.

That flexibility applies to operational systems as well as physical laboratories. New instruments and research methods emerge, user communities change, and facilities develop new requirements. An open-source platform allows individual facilities to respond to those changes while providing a mechanism for improvements to be shared.

At MIT.nano alone, NEMO supports more than 1,600 active researchers using more than 200 tools, with approximately 160,000 hours of tool usage each year. For Jorg Scholvin, associate director of Fab.nano, operating at that scale makes the efficiency of everyday processes, and the ability to adapt and change quickly, important.

“A small improvement in an administrative workflow can be multiplied across thousands of users and tens of thousands of equipment interactions,” he said.

The NEMO wave

The sense of community and positive outlook for the future of shared facilities was apparent throughout the two-day meeting. Closing discussions looked ahead to the role of data integration, automation, and artificial intelligence in lab operations.

“The community is taking on a life of its own,” said Mathieu Rampant, CEO and co-founder of Atlantis Labs, describing a model in which facility managers can share ideas and solve problems together. “It’s more sustainable,” he added as he talked about having to do less as the NEMO-CE manager because the facilities managers are talking to each other — sharing ideas and solving problems as a network: “the NEMO wave,” Samantha Roberts, director of the City University of New York nanofabrication facility, called it. “Everyone is invested in it and cares about it. It takes a lot of effort to change your lab management system and if we keep this going, we can build out something that’s really cool and that works.”

For Osherov, the purpose remains straightforward.

“Ultimately, this is about enabling research. The better we can manage the operational side of our facilities, the more effectively we can make our instruments, expertise, and capabilities available to the research community.”

In microelectronics, where innovation increasingly depends on access to specialized and distributed capabilities, that availability matters. The ability to find the right capability at the right facility, using information drawn directly from actively used systems, can help researchers move more quickly from an idea to an experiment to real-world application and impact.

articles.author: Walid El Houri
articles.title: Egypt’s crackdown on independent media reaches Mada Masr as editor faces trial
articles.excerpt: Egypt convicted Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations, and ordered it closed
articles.content:
This story by Walid El Houri originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

Egypt convicted Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations, and ordered it closed

A crackdown on independent media in Egypt is escalating.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists. 

The six-person team was forcibly disappeared, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news. They remain in pretrial detention.

The crackdown then reached Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah. On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.

The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license, in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial. She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later. The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.

According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected. The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes. 

Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.

Mada Masr was founded in 2013 as an independent, critical, investigative outlet. In another decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region. It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights. 

Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.

An attack on journalism

The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism. At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday, October 30, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.” A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.

“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about. But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads. It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.” It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.

Solidarity and journalism

In an op-ed published on October 26, the Mada Masr team wrote that “in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday.”

They added: “There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism.”

And: “We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small us, Mada Masr, but a much bigger we.”

In Egypt, journalists who documented torture, political imprisonment, and security crackdowns now face courts that process them quickly and unfairly, under a licensing scheme that has left applicants without an answer for years.

For journalism to be free, that licensing scheme and its chilling effects on access to information, knowledge production, and critical voices in Egypt and beyond must be stopped.

Written by Walid El Houri

articles.title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: The Secret Room
articles.excerpt: The government’s surveillance powers grew rapidly after Sept. 11, 2001, some in public view and some in secret. articles.content:
Josh Richman · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

The government’s surveillance powers grew rapidly after Sept. 11, 2001, some in public view and some in secret. EFF suspected but couldn’t prove that the National Security Agency was spying on Americans' communications. The New York Times sat on a story about it for over a year, finally publishing it in December 2005. Then, in January 2006, a retired AT&T technician named Mark Klein walked into EFF's office with a manila folder of documents that blew the story wide open. 

Welcome to the third episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.

%3Ciframe%20height%3D%2252px%22%20width%3D%22100%25%22%20frameborder%3D%22no%22%20scrolling%3D%22no%22%20seamless%3D%22%22%20src%3D%22https%3A%2F%2Fplayer.simplecast.com%2Fe7dd937c-3319-4a9a-9245-f9ed34b9419d%3Fdark%3Dtrue%26amp%3Bcolor%3D000000%22%20allow%3D%22autoplay%22%3E%3C%2Fiframe%3E Privacy info. This embed will serve content from simplecast.com

   

(You can also find this episode on YouTube.)

In this episode, former EFF Executive Director Cindy Cohn talks with former EFF lawyer Kevin Bankston, who was at his desk drafting a lawsuit against AT&T when Klein showed up. Less than two weeks later, EFF sued the phone company on behalf of its own customers in Hepting v. AT&T. Cindy speaks again with now-retired Justice Department lawyer Tony Coppolino, who asked for the opportunity to defend the case. He called EFF with a warning after Klein’s documents were filed in court: If they were classified, EFF would be in big trouble. You’ll also hear from Klein himself, and from Carolyn Jewel, a romance novelist and AT&T customer who became the lead plaintiff in EFF's related case against the NSA. 

It's the story of a secret room in a San Francisco phone company building, a heroic whistleblower, and the people who refused to let mass surveillance stay hidden. 

The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so pick up your copy today!  

Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast.   

Jarrod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it.   

Corinne Ruff is our story editor. 

We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman. 

The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.

articles.author: Timothée Ravier
articles.title: What’s New for Fedora Atomic Desktops in Fedora Linux 45
articles.excerpt: Fedora 45 is now available! So let’s see what this new release for the Fedora Atomic Desktops variants includes for Silverblue, Kinoite, Sway Atomic, Budgie Atomic and COSMIC Atomic.
articles.content:
Timothée Ravier · Fedora Magazine · CC BY-SA 4.0

Fedora 45 is now available! So let’s see what this new release for the Fedora Atomic Desktops variants includes for Silverblue, Kinoite, Sway Atomic, Budgie Atomic and COSMIC Atomic.

Changes for all Atomic Desktops

Completed the migration to the new Fedora forge

Everything related to the Atomic Desktops now resides in the atomic-desktops organization.

The only remaining repo on GitLab.com/fedora is the one used to build the unofficial bootable container images (gitlab.com/fedora/ostree/ci-test). The migration of this repo will occur in the future, as well.

Anaconda Web UI

The Atomic Desktops installer ISOs now use the new Anaconda WebUI. This follows the same change that occurred for Fedora Workstation 42 and Fedora 43 Spins.

This also enables remote installation of a system using a Web browser on another machine over HTTPS.

See the Fedora Change pages for the switch to the WebUI and for Web based remote installations.

Installer images (ISO) and disk images built by Image Builder

The installer images (ISO) are now built by Image Builder. While there should not be any immediate visible changes, this will help us move to the bootable container images in the future.

This also enables us to offer pre-installed disk images for Silverblue and Kinoite. Those images are currently in preview and only those variants are covered for now. They are the only ones with a first boot experience from a disk image.

See the Fedora Change page for further information.

General Fedora changes worth noting

The following changes are part of the general set of changes that come with Fedora Linux 45 and are worth noting for Atomic Desktops users:

  • Podman 6.0 & 6.1: The latest version of the container management tool. See the blog posts:
    • Introducing Podman v6.0.0
    • Podman 6 Configuration File Changes
    • Podman 6.1.0: Volume Renaming, Machine Restarts, and a Long List of Bug Fixes
    • Support for slirp4netns and the BoltDB backend have been removed.
  • oo7 Secrets Service Provider: New secrets backend, enabled for all variants at the exception of Kinoite.
  • DRM Panic Frontend: An easier way to report kernel crashes using a web interface. Hopefully you will never see it!

What’s new in Silverblue

Fedora Silverblue comes with the latest GNOME 51 release.

For more details about the changes alongside GNOME 51, see What’s new in Fedora Workstation 45 on the Fedora Magazine.

What’s new in Kinoite

Fedora Kinoite ships with Plasma 6.7, Frameworks 6.31 and Gear 26.08.

Plasma 6.8 is expected to land right after the release.

See also What’s new in Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop 45 on the Fedora Magazine.

What’s new in Sway Atomic

Fedora Sway Atomic comes with the latest 1.12 Sway release.

What’s new in Budgie Atomic

Fedora Budgie Atomic comes with the brand new version 10.10.3 of Budgie Desktop: New Favorites in Budgie Menu, re-introduced Keyboard applet with Wayland support, massive improvements to our desktop view, primary monitor selection, and more! See the 10.10.3 Budgie release announcement.

What’s new in COSMIC Atomic

Fedora COSMIC Atomic comes with the 1.10.0 release of the COSMIC desktop.

Universal Blue, Bluefin, Bazzite, Aurora and secureblue

Our friends in the Universal Blue project (Bazzite, Bluefin, Aurora) have prepared the update to Fedora 45. Look for upcoming announcements in their Discourse.

As always, I heavily recommend checking them out, especially if you feel like some things are missing from the Fedora Atomic Desktops and you depend on them (NVIDIA drivers, extra media codec, out of tree kernel drivers, etc.).

If you have an interest in more security focused variants, I recommend taking a look at the secureblue project.

What’s next

Roadmap to Bootable Containers and bootc / CoreOS / Atomic unification

A lot of work is happening to make the transition to Bootable Containers as smooth as possible for our existing users. You can look at the roadmap for this transition at atomic-desktops#26.

Most of the progress in this release cycle was (again) focused on getting our bootable container images ready for general consumption in Fedora. A part of this work is being able to build them reliably in the Fedora Infra.

The people involved in the bootc, CoreOS and other Atomic variants are working on this effort as part of the new Atomic SIG. See atomic#137 and the project board.

Making it easier to derive images into Fedora Remix images

Work is in progress to make it easier to create derived container images from the Fedora Atomic Desktops images, notably in order to comply with the logo and branding policy.

Once this is ready, we may start publishing “Fedora Remix” branded container images of the Fedora Atomic Desktops. Those images will not include official Fedora branding and will thus be better suited for projects that want to layer their changes on top.

See atomic-desktops#125 and atomic-desktops#132.

Helping us with a few nasty bugs

If you have an interest in contributing to Fedora Atomic Desktops, here are some bugs that we will have to fix in the short term. We would greatly appreciate help with the following issues from the ticket tracker:

  • Fixing root mount options (atomic-desktops#72): This is a long standing and mostly invisible bug that impacts performance.
  • Moving away from nss-altfiles (atomic-desktops#108): This is another long standing source of issues that new users regularly face.

Where to reach us

We are looking for contributors to help us make the Fedora Atomic Desktops the best experience for Fedora users. The following are Matrix rooms that may be of interest to potential contributors:

  • Atomic Desktops SIG: Organization on Fedora’s Forge, #atomic-desktops:fedoraproject.org
  • Silverblue: Workstation Working Group, #silverblue:fedoraproject.org
  • Kinoite: KDE SIG, #kinoite:fedoraproject.org
  • Sway Atomic: Sway SIG, #sway:fedoraproject.org
  • Budgie Atomic: Budgie SIG, #budgie:fedoraproject.org
  • COSMIC Atomic: COSMIC SIG, #cosmic:fedoraproject.org

articles.author: Michal Konečný
articles.title: How to Rebase to Fedora Linux 45 on Silverblue
articles.excerpt: Fedora Silverblue is an operating system for your desktop built on Fedora Linux. It’s excellent for daily use, development, and container-based workflows. It offers numerous advantages such as being able to roll back in case of any problems. If you want to rebase to Fedora Linux 45 on your Fedora Silverblue system, this article tells you how. It not only shows you what to do, but also how to revert things if something unforeseen happens.
articles.content:
Michal Konečný · Fedora Magazine · CC BY-SA 4.0

Fedora Silverblue is an operating system for your desktop built on Fedora Linux. It’s excellent for daily use, development, and container-based workflows. It offers numerous advantages such as being able to roll back in case of any problems. If you want to rebase to Fedora Linux 45 on your Fedora Silverblue system, this article tells you how. It not only shows you what to do, but also how to revert things if something unforeseen happens.

Update your existing system

Prior to actually doing the rebase to Fedora Linux 45, you should apply any pending updates. Enter the following in the terminal:

$ rpm-ostree update

or install updates through GNOME Software and reboot.

Note

rpm-ostree is the underlying atomic technology that all the Fedora Atomic Desktops use. The techniques described here for Silverblue will apply to all of them with proper modifications for the appropriate desktop.

Rebasing using GNOME Software

GNOME Software shows you that there is new version of Fedora Linux available on the Updates screen.

First thing to do is download the new image, so select the Download button. This will take some time. When it is done you will see that the update is ready to install.

Select the Restart & Upgrade button. This step will take only a few moments and the computer will restart when the update has completed. After the restart you will end up in a new and shiny release of Fedora Linux 45. Easy, isn’t it?

Rebasing using terminal

If you prefer to do everything in a terminal, then this part of the guide is for you.

Rebasing to Fedora Linux 45 using the terminal is easy. First, check if the 45 branch is available:

$ ostree remote refs fedora

You should see the following in the output:

fedora:fedora/45/x86_64/silverblue

If you want to pin the current deployment (meaning that this deployment will stay as an option in GRUB until you remove it), you can do this by running this command:

# 0 is entry position in rpm-ostree status
$ sudo ostree admin pin 0

To remove the pinned deployment use the following command:

# 2 is entry position in rpm-ostree status 
$ sudo ostree admin pin --unpin 2

Next, rebase your system to the Fedora Linux 45 branch.

$ rpm-ostree rebase fedora:fedora/45/x86_64/silverblue

Finally, the last thing to do is restart your computer and boot to Fedora Linux 45.

How to roll back

If anything bad happens (for instance, if you can’t boot to Fedora Linux 45 at all) it’s easy to go back. At boot time, pick the entry in the GRUB menu for the version prior to Fedora Linux 45 and your system will start in that previous version rather than Fedora Linux 45. If you don’t see the GRUB menu, try to press ESC during boot. To make the change to the previous version permanent, use the following command:

$ rpm-ostree rollback

That’s it. Now you know how to rebase Fedora Silverblue to Fedora Linux 45 and roll back. So why not do it today?

FAQ

Because there are similar questions in comments for each blog about rebasing to newer version of Silverblue I will try to answer them in this section.

Question: Can I skip versions during a rebase of Fedora Linux? For example from Fedora Silverblue 42 to Fedora Silverblue 45?

Answer: Although it could sometimes be possible to skip versions during rebase, it is not recommended. You should always update to one version prior (42->43->44->45 for example) to avoid unnecessary errors.

Question: I have rpm-fusion layered and I get errors during rebase. How should I do the rebase?

Answer: If you have rpm-fusion layered on your Silverblue installation, you should do the following before rebase:

$ rpm-ostree update --uninstall rpmfusion-free-release --uninstall rpmfusion-nonfree-release --install rpmfusion-free-release --install rpmfusion-nonfree-release

After doing this you can follow the guide in this blog post.

Question: Could this guide be used for other ostree editions (Fedora Atomic Desktops) as well like Kinoite, Sericea (Sway Atomic), Onyx (Budgie Atomic),…?

Yes, you can follow the Rebasing using the terminal part of this guide for every Fedora Atomic Desktop. Just use the corresponding branch. For example, for Kinoite use fedora:fedora/45/x86_64/kinoite

articles.author: Aoife Moloney
articles.title: What’s New in Fedora Workstation 45
articles.excerpt: Fedora Workstation features the latest six months of meticulous polish, under-the-hood responsiveness, and security hardening for F45, based on GNOME 51. Whether you are multitasking across monitors, managing daily appointments, or organizing large sets of files, GNOME 51 brings thoughtful refinements to your daily workflow on Fedora Workstation.
articles.content:
Aoife Moloney · Fedora Magazine · CC BY-SA 4.0

Fedora Workstation features the latest six months of meticulous polish, under-the-hood responsiveness, and security hardening for F45, based on GNOME 51. Whether you are multitasking across monitors, managing daily appointments, or organizing large sets of files, GNOME 51 brings thoughtful refinements to your daily workflow on Fedora Workstation.

Silky-Smooth Responsiveness: Reworked Frame Scheduling

One standout improvement in GNOME 51 is a reworked frame scheduling and frame delivery system in Mutter. Animations, window snapping, and desktop transitions now hold a rock-steady frame rate even when the CPU and GPU are under heavy compile or gaming loads.

In tandem with this, GNOME streamlined its graphics pipeline by retiring legacy NVIDIA proprietary interfaces in favor of the standard GBM memory management path. This makes Wayland sessions cleaner, faster, and more uniform across all hardware.

Everyday App Polish

Files (Nautilus) Gets Quality-of-Life Upgrades

Files has picked up several subtle but indispensable touches:

  • Drag-and-Drop Counter Badge: When selecting and dragging multiple files, a small badge now shows the exact count of items you’re moving.
  • Non-Blocking Operations: Large or slow directory reloads no longer freeze the interface, resulting in a snappier file management experience.
  • Notification Grouping: Grouping status and operation notifications together now keeps your notification tray tidy.

Calendar Rebuilt for Speed

Calendar feels faster than ever. The entire view-rendering engine was overhauled under the hood. This dramatically cut down the lag when scrolling through dense schedules in Month View. Reorganization within the event editor now presents a cleaner Notes section and native recognition of modern video conference links.

Revamped File Previewer

The quick-look File Previewer received a top-to-bottom redesign built on modern GTK 4 and libadwaita. It now seamlessly matches your desktop theme, respects Dark Style, handles fractional display scaling crisper than before, and properly previews high-resolution images at their actual native size.

Deeper Security: Next-Generation Secret Storage with oo7

Security underpins everything in Fedora Workstation. GNOME 51 introduces oo7, a modern Secret Service provider written from scratch to safely store application passwords, API tokens, and credentials.

Fedora Workstation is replacing legacy keyring daemons with a compartmentalized, sandboxed service. This provides even stronger defense against rogue applications attempting to peek at cached user credentials.

Accessibility and Navigation Upgrades

  • Keyboard-Driven Screenshots: You can now adjust screenshot selection boxes entirely with your arrow keys ( Alt to move the selection, Shift / Ctrl for coarse/fine resizing, and R to reset).
  • Extended Reduced Motion: Toggling the Reduced Motion accessibility option now softens animations across more core widgets and Shell elements than ever before.
  • Reorganized Settings: The About (System Details) panel now includes a direct button to view the release notes for your running GNOME version, alongside a revamped fingerprint enrollment flow.

Upgrade or Try Fedora Workstation

If you’re already running Fedora, upgrading through GNOME Software or via the terminal with

dnf system-upgrade will bring you right into GNOME 51. For clean installs, check out the Fedora Workstation live media at getfedora.org.

Share your favorite new feature or thoughts on the release over at the Fedora Discussion forum!

Disclaimer: Google Gemini, using the GNOME 51 release notes, assisted in the creation of this article. It was reviewed by humans before publishing. No apparent hallucinations were noted, however ,some content was not included.

Please read the GNOME 51 release notes for even more cool features that you can enjoy on Fedora Workstation as part of the F45 release.

articles.title: What’s New in Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop 45
articles.excerpt: KDE Plasma 6.8 was released on KDE’s 30 year anniversary and we are proud to have it be the star of Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop Edition 45.
articles.content:
Troy Dawson · Fedora Magazine · CC BY-SA 4.0

KDE Plasma 6.8 was released on KDE’s 30 year anniversary and we are proud to have it be the star of Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop Edition 45.

The Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop Edition is well suited for many needs. It combines the reliable and trusted Fedora Linux base with the KDE Plasma Desktop environment. It provides a selection of KDE applications that are simple by default, but powerful when needed.

KDE Plasma 6.8

KDE developers continue to release new features, fix bugs and fine-tune the desktop experience to improve on the now well-established foundation of Plasma 6. There have been two KDE Plasma releases since our last Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop Edition shipped. Some of the new features and updates include:

New Features

  • Per-screen virtual desktops: After 21 years per-screen virtual desktops have finally arrived!
  • Test your microphone volume: Stop wondering if it’s your microphone or an app that’s misbehaving.
  • Press-and-hold for special characters: With Plasma’s virtual keyboard enabled, press and hold a key to type special characters related to it.
  • Light/dark mode toggle: A quick toggle in the system tray to switch between light and dark Global Themes immediately.
  • “Background Apps” in the System Tray: The system tray now shows apps using the newer “Background Apps” system, which is more common for apps using the Flatpak package format.

Updated Features

  • Better Accessibility: a new “dwell clicker” feature can send a mouse click when the pointer stops moving. Designed especially for users with mobility issues.
  • Remote Desktop: Much better performance and quality, bi-directional clipboard synchronization, exclusive mode and overall polish to the experience.
  • Printing: Now the System Tray icon for printers shows the number of active jobs in a little badge.
  • Faster virtual desktop switching in the Overview: When you press “Meta + W” to open the Overview screen, Plasma now lets you switch virtual desktops simply by scrolling or pressing the “Page Up” or “Page Down” keys.
  • Easier to compare different time zones: The Digital Clock widget lets you add multiple time zones and quickly compare them.

Theming

  • Oxygen: For KDE’s 30th anniversary the Oxygen theme is back and brought up to par.
  • Breeze: The default Breeze theme also continues to evolve, now featuring rounded list and grid view highlights for many applications, and visible click effects for menu items.
  • Union: Plasma’s all-new Union theming system streamlines theming by making it possible to style Plasma, QtQuick apps, and QtWidgets apps all with a single set of easy-to-write CSS.

And More …

There is so much new stuff since our last Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop Edition was released. Check out the full release announcements for Plasma 6.7 and Plasma 6.8.

Fedora Linux 45 general updates

Some broader changes in Fedora Linux also directly impact Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop Edition, notably:

  • Updated Podman: Podman 6 includes new features, but also significant API and CLI breaking changes. Depending on how you use Podman, this change may significantly affect you. The Podman 6 change proposal has information on what is affected.
  • NetworkManager VPN: NetworkManager-vpnc and NetworkManager-fortisslvpn are not in Fedora 45. If you already have them installed and are updating to Fedora 45, NetworkManager will obsolete and remove them. Users still using them should migrate their connection profiles to openconnect or libreswan.
  • Lazarus with multiple widget sets: The lazarus-ide now comes with a Qt6 option in lazarus-ide-qt6.
  • Updated IBus: IBus now supports the ISO latch and shift states of XKB key-maps in Wayland desktop environments like KDE, Sway, Hyprland, COSMIC.
  • DRM Panic Frontend: The DRM Panic Frontend provides users with a user-friendly interface for understanding kernel panic information and facilitates bug reports.

Wrap-up

The Fedora KDE SIG hopes that you’ll find Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop 45 to be a wonderful experience. When you’re ready to try it, click here for download links and verification instructions. If you would like to learn more, check out the Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop website.

articles.author: Oiwan Lam
articles.title: Unpacking Hong Kong’s rule of law score according to the World Justice Project’s ranking
articles.excerpt: Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down
articles.content:
This story by Oiwan Lam originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “Rule of Law Index 2026” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice. That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific. Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”

Best performance: “order and security” and “absence of corruption”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score). Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth). 

In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests. However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations. 

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report, which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector. Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights. Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.

Worst performance: “constraints in government's power” and “fundamental rights”

Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score). 

Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026. The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020, which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges. Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred. Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

The report described the “constraints in government’s power” performance as moderately to alarmingly risky, with constraints from the legislature ranking 84, judiciary 64, independent auditing and review bodies 61, non-government organizations 105, and the law 90 — the law refers to the legal framework that protects procedural justice and integrity regarding the appointment of officials and the electoral process. As for the subfactor “official sanctioned for misconduct,” which has a fair 22 ranking, some Hongkongers may consider the score too generous given that only one official has taken responsibility and resigned over the preventable Taipo Fire disaster.

A similar downward trend appears in the “fundamental rights” category, which ranked 29th in 2015, slipped to 38th in 2020, plummeted to 54th in 2021, and fell to 69th in 2026. The at-risk subfactors include security of suspects and dissidents (73), freedom of opinion and expression (105), privacy protection (86), freedom of assembly and association (115), and labor rights (66).

Hong Kong saw the shutdown of Apple Daily News and Stand News in 2021 upon the enactment of the National Security Law in 2020. The domestic Article 23 security law was enacted in March 2024 to further clamp down on “soft resistance” with the newly introduced sedition crime. Privacy rights have declined, as implementation rules for national security laws have empowered police to conduct physical searches of private property and digital devices without court warrants during national security investigations. Since 2020, NGOs, independent media outlets, and activist groups have vanished en masse amid a tightening political environment and shrinking civic space for organizational activities.

The fairly ranked subfactors are freedom from discrimination (29), rights of the accused and convicted (32), and freedom of religion (31).

Poor performance on “fundamental rights” also drags down the “open government” factor's rank (29), with its subfactor “civic participation” ranking 87 in an at-risk level.

Downgraded “civil justice” and “criminal justice”

Although Hong Kong's overall performance in civil and criminal justice remains fair, both factors have fallen from their historical high ranks of 11th and 7th to the current 20th and 23rd. 

The main subfactors driving the decline in civil justice are discrimination (48) and improper government influence (56).

After the passage of Legal Aid Reforms in 2021, the number of applications to fund judicial review that challenge the government’s policy and decisions received by the Legal Aid Department dropped 60 percent from around  275 in 2016 to 110 in 2025. Of those 110 requests, the department approved only 2 cases. The overall number of judicial review cases fell from a peak of 3,899 in 2019 to 1,545 in 2022. Because most cases involve non-refoulement claims for refugee status, the government, in addition to the administrative Unified Screening Mechanism (USM) launched in 2014, introduced a special scheme in March 2025 to appoint eligible private practitioners as Deputy Judges of the Court of First Instance to handle these cases exclusively. The mechanism disposed of more than 3700 claims in 2025. Both reforms, driven by the government administration's political considerations, have negatively affected the poor and the non-citizen's access to judicial justice in Hong Kong. 

The major subfactor contributing to the fall in criminal justice ranking is “government or political influence on the criminal justice system” (61).

Hong Kong’s criminal justice ranking first plunged in 2017, from 8th to 16th, after the government labeled the civil unrest in Mong Kok, dubbed the Fishball Revolution, as a riot and reactivated the colonial-era Public Order Ordinance to prosecute protesters en masse. Then, in 2021 and 2022, the ranking dropped again amid a series of speech-related national security prosecutions against 47 pro-democracy activists for participating in the primaries of the election of the legislature for conspiracy to subvert, Apple Daily senior executives for foreign collusion, and Stand News editors for conspiracy to publish seditious content. The recent convictions and heavy sentencing of Apple Daily’s executives, including Jimmy Lai, and former leaders over collusion, Albert Ho Chun-yan, Lee Chuek-yan and Chow Hang-tung, of the now-disbanded organizer of the June 4th candlelight vigil, Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, over inciting subversion, may further downgrade the city’s criminal justice performance in the next year. The fact that all these controversial cases were handled by judges designated by the Chief Executive adds weight to the evaluation of “government or political influence on the criminal justice system”.

According to the Index’s insights, the global rule of law has declined for 9 consecutive years. Civic participation and the freedoms of speech and assembly each fell in over 60 percent of countries, and Hong Kong is among them. The city also sees the global trend of improper government influence that undermines civil and criminal justice.

The Rule of Law Index is particularly crucial to global financial centers; as the WJP notes, when the index scores reach 0.66, countries tend to have high sovereign credit ratings. Currently, Hong Kong’s score is 0.71 and trending down, while its Asian competitor, Singapore, ranks 14th with a 0.79 score and an upward trend. Watchdogs indicate this could be a bad sign for the city as it seeks to secure its spot as the region’s top economy.

Written by Oiwan Lam

articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
articles.title: In Kosovo, a new app makes reporting problems to the government fast and easy
articles.excerpt: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions
articles.content:
This story by Nurbek Bekmurzaev originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy. Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government.  Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.

Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation. Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.

We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology. This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.

The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project? 

HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.

This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.

Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind. The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.

Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project? 

HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

Beyond the platform, Sbunker has served as a capacity hub for other Digital Sparks project grantees during the project period. We organized meetings and an advocacy workshop where grantees worked on developing a joint advocacy event.

We also hosted a young fellow, Bora Dibra, from the Albanian organization IRSH (Young Intellectuals, Hope), for a one-month fellowship focused on digital civic engagement, media literacy, and participatory advocacy.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

HD: The project has allowed Sbunker to expand the way we approach civic engagement. Much of our work traditionally focused on informing citizens and creating public debate through publications.

Through Kosovo.report, we are developing a tool that takes this a step further by giving citizens a channel through which they can raise problems in their communities and have their reports directed to the relevant departments.

The next step will be the pilot of Kosovo.report in the capital, Prishtina, where we will be able to test the platform with citizens, gather their feedback, and identify what needs to be improved.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

HD: Developing Kosovo.report has given us experience in creating a digital tool through which citizens can report issues and direct them to the relevant departments.

The process has also involved working with the Municipality of Prishtina as we prepare for the pilot phase of the project, which is a different scope of work from Sbunker's focus on media and public debate.

Our role as a capacity hub has also given us an opportunity to work more closely with individual grantees and other civil society organizations, learn about their projects in digital democracy, and the challenges in their communities.

Taken together, these activities have expanded Sbunker’s experience from media, analysis and public debate, to developing digital tools and working more closely with civil society organizations and public institutions.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

HD: One of the most valuable experiences has been developing something that is intended to have a direct use in people’s everyday lives. With Kosovo.report, we are taking a different approach by developing a platform that citizens can use in their communities and communicate with relevant institutions.

Building the platform has also given us a better sense of what it takes to turn an idea for civic participation into something that works in practice.

The capacity hub and fellowship have added to this experience by allowing us to work with people approaching digital democracy and civic engagement from different projects and contexts.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

HD: For us, Kosovo.report is a starting point for what we want to do in the digital democracy area. The current focus is on Prishtina, but we want to take the platform beyond the pilot and explore opportunities to connect with other municipalities and public institutions across Kosovo.

The first phase is helping us see what works, what needs to be improved, and how the platform can better respond to the needs of local communities.

The project has also strengthened Sbunker’s capacity to develop digital approaches to civic participation. We want to build on that experience in our future work by looking more closely at the needs of the communities we work with and explore where digital tools can help address them.

We also want to continue the relationships developed through this project, both with civil society organizations and collaborators, and see where they can lead beyond the project.

Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev

articles.author: Leda Zimmerman | MIT Energy Initiative
articles.title: Powering up for a pivotal moment
articles.excerpt: From a nuclear revival to qubits, the MIT Energy Initiative’s annual research conference tracked deployment of today’s technologies to discovery of tomorrow’s breakthroughs.
articles.content:
Leda Zimmerman | MIT Energy Initiative · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

From a nuclear revival to qubits, the MIT Energy Initiative’s annual research conference tracked deployment of today’s technologies to discovery of tomorrow’s breakthroughs.

Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23.

The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.” 

More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions.

With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond. 

From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories.

Deploying today’s technologies

Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy. 

“We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said.

The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow. 

There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power. 

Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario.

Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO2.

Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said. 

Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store energy.

“The pace of the transition to a renewable-energy economy will strongly rely on the availability of scalable, bulk energy-storage solutions,” said Masic.

Kripa K. Varanasi, a professor in the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, is working on ways to make technologies such as emissions-plume capture at power plants economically viable. 

In a panel devoted to startups with links to MITEI or MITEI member companies, speakers described moving novel energy technologies from research to commercialization: Alfredo Rivela of Adaion has developed an AI tool for electrical utilities that optimizes their use of the grid; Eddie Obropta of Raptor Maps trains drones to inspect solar farms; Michele Guarnieri’s HiBot has created a robot that detects issues in power lines; and Michael Wang of Lithios is conducting field pilots that use electrochemistry to separate lithium from low-grade brines.

Successful ventures, the speakers agreed, begin with a clear customer problem that can be validated by industry users and that offers a path to scaled deployment. For industry users, “innovation is not a corporate virtue,” said Steve Hellman, managing partner at Alliance Partners. “It’s an existential requirement.”

Early-stage research and basic science

The conference also offered a bounty of promising early research on technologies and approaches for cutting carbon emissions. A panel on MITEI’s Seed Innovation Fund Program projects introduced MIT scientists who are separating and recycling rare earth elements; designing algorithms to decide which power plants should run to meet electricity demand; and modeling the impacts on human and natural systems of development and decarbonization.

A poster session revealed the next generation of energy researchers in such fields as chemistry, architecture, aeronautics and astronautics, and computer science. Graduate students are developing a wide array of technologies for carbon mitigation and new energy systems, such as a steam electrolysis process for hydrogen production; models of end-to-end decarbonization in buildings; and designs for hydrogen- and methane-fueled aircraft.

The conference highlighted the importance of fundamental science in feeding the pipeline of new energy technologies. Wednesday’s keynote speaker, Danna Freedman, the F. G. Keyes Professor of Chemistry at MIT and inaugural director of the MIT Quantum Initiative (QMIT), traced scientists’ evolving capacity to harness quantum computing as a tool for solving a range of problems, including those in energy.

“What we want to do at QMIT is solve the hard problem, and the hard problem isn’t developing these ridiculously intricate and beautiful quantum tools,” said Freedman. “It is connecting the quantum tools with the applications that will change the world.”

A companion panel explored one such application: quantum sensing, which leverages fundamental physics to capture a nanoscale view of materials and their properties. For instance, Lukasz Zielinski, scientific advisor to the Integrated Sensing and Measurement Program at SLB, uses a lidar camera with single-photon detectors to identify methane plumes. Moderator Paola Cappellaro, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, described her work using diamond-based sensors for detecting tiny magnetic fields from battery current, potentially helping measure battery conditions without disturbing the battery electrically. Such quantum sensors, Cappellaro said, can be “practical and impactful.” 

Data centers and public trust

One critical challenge facing energy researchers and industry emerged in sessions throughout the two days: the explosive growth of AI and the energy-hungry data centers that fuel this technology. As Deepjyoti Deka, a MITEI principal research scientist, put it, “the big test for AI right now is whether AI can reduce energy usage, improve efficiency, as well as bring in innovation faster than the rate at which it is going to consume electricity to get trained and deployed.” 

“New ‘hyperscale’ facilities built for artificial intelligence can use more power than entire cities,” said Steve Clemmer, director of energy research in the Climate and Energy Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, sharing a recent analysis of data center proliferation. With new facilities being 10 to even 10,000 times larger than data centers built just a decade ago, he said, wholesale electricity costs will rise, and “increased reliance on fossil fuels will result in tens of billions of dollars in health damages, and trillions in climate damages.” He noted that decision-makers can mitigate these harmful impacts through clean energy development, strong ratepayer protections, and other safeguards.

Given mounting opposition to data centers, Kathryn Kline Tyndall, associate director of energy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, recommended that industry proponents provide early, accessible information about power, water, quality-of-life, land-use, environmental, and economic impacts, tailored to each community in which they hope to set up shop.

Larry Susskind, the Ford Professor of Urban and Environmental Planning in the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, recommended that developers go further, and demonstrate credible benefits to communities. To achieve this, Susskind suggests a facilitated negotiation process between developers and local groups whose object is a community benefits agreement — a deal that might involve altering the data center design, and providing workforce development, infrastructure investment, and clean energy partnerships.

Ultimately, developers must accept that they can’t rush community acceptance; they have to earn it by giving residents a meaningful role in shaping projects and sharing their benefits. 

“You’re going to have to proceed at the speed of trust,” said Susskind.

articles.author: Civic Media Observatory
articles.title: The Brazilian left’s quest to ‘tame’ Meta: A narrative of denouncement and resistance
articles.excerpt: Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning
articles.content:
This story by Civic Media Observatory originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning

This story is part of Undertones, Global Voices’ Civic Media Observatory’s newsletter and column. Subscribe to Undertones here. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Over the years, Meta’s content moderation policies and governance practices have faced intense scrutiny and legal challenges over alleged political bias and a lack of transparency.

Since 2018, the Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), a human rights organization advocating for Palestinian digital rights, has documented how Facebook’s (now Meta) moderation practices disproportionately affect Palestinian content. In 2020, 7amleh launched a campaign challenging Facebook’s proposed hate speech policy, which considered “Zionist” a potential proxy for “Jew” or “Jewish.” More recently, in 2024, the organization collected 20 first-hand testimonies from Palestinian influencers, journalists, and media outlets documenting their experiences of Meta’s discriminatory content moderation practices. In 2023, Human Rights Watch also reported “systemic online censorship” against voices in support of Palestine and Palestinian human rights,

In 2022, Tom Vandendriessche, a Belgian politician and Member of the European Parliament (MEP) representing the far-right Vlaams Belang (Flemish Interest) party, partially prevailed in a legal case against Meta concerning a shadow ban imposed on his account in 2021 after the company removed several posts alleging a breach of its Terms of Service (ToS) and Facebook Community Guidelines (FCG). A Belgian court ordered the company to compensate the politician for financial and reputational damages, finding that its actions had significantly restricted his ability to engage in political discourse online and that Meta had failed to provide adequate transparency or effective avenues for redress.

In 2026, Meta has faced significant criticism in Brazil and internationally from internet rights watchdogs over political bias, algorithmic interference, and the selective suppression of content perceived as favoring far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro during the October 2026 Brazilian presidential election.

Narrative: Meta, take your hands off our election!

Using the slogan Meta não se meta (roughly, “Meta, stay out of it”), which plays on the Portuguese word meta, derived from the verb meter (“to get involved” or “to interfere”), internet rights defenders and current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s followers and allies sought not only to expose alleged Meta’s shadow-banning practices during Brazil’s 2026 presidential election but also to mobilize Brazilians to demand a fairer digital space collectively. 

Sub-narrative: We demand digital sovereignty, and we will hold Meta accountable

In October 2026, during the Brazilian presidential runoff election campaign, a coalition of Brazilian civil society organizations, social movements, and digital rights advocacy groups, including CTRL+Z, Código Não Binário, ARTIGO 19 (Article 19 Brasil), Sleeping Giants Brasil, and others, launched the webpage naosemeta.com.br as part of their initiative to denounce electoral interference and algorithmic bias. The site offered three ways for people to hold Meta accountable online: email Meta; message Meta’s General Director in Brazil on LinkedIn; and comment on Meta Ceo Mark Zuckerberg’s latest Instagram post. It also shared a space for those wishing to join and sign a petition to the Superior Electoral Court and an extrajudicial notification, a formal written communication sent on October 19 to put Meta on notice and demand that it recognize the technical flaws in its advertising, moderation, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and the distribution and availability of user-generated content and campaign materials in Brazil — which these organizations claim disadvantaged, in particular, candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The online strategy to hold Meta accountable was accompanied by a protest in front of Meta’s offices on October 19, where participants called for respect for Brazil’s digital sovereignty, with the Homeless Workers Movement’s Technology Center among the loudest voices.

For those reclaiming digital sovereignty, the company’s actions stem from the relationship between U.S. President Donald Trump and Brazil’s ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, father of Flávio Bolsonaro, and the influence the current U.S. administration has over big-tech owners — they consider Meta to be facilitating foreign interference.

Sub-narrative: Together, we can “tame” the algorithm

An extra layer supported the narrative “Meta, take your hands off our election!” After the first round of the election gave candidate Flávio Bolsonaro a small lead in early October, left-wing Congressman André Janones relaunched his WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army,” an initiative to mobilize voters online and offline and give visibility to Lula da Silva’s messaging and proposals, and that quickly gained millions of followers.

In addition to reclaiming Brazilian symbols from the far-right, including inviting followers to wear the country’s yellow soccer team T-shirt, the WhatsApp channel coordinated social media interactions to boost Lula da Silva’s visibility. By giving his “troops” instructions on when and how to engage with the content Lula da Silva’s campaign produced, Janones positioned an implicit narrative that argued it was possible to “tame” the algorithm, regain ownership of the Brazilian digital media ecosystem, and ultimately win the election, recapturing the campaign spirits.

After Lula da Silva’s unprecedented second-round comeback on October 25, this narrative evolved to “dobramos a Meta,” which translates to “we doubled Meta,” hinting at the “dobrar a meta” (doubled the target) popular meme that originated from a statement made by former Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff in July 2015, during a speech on the National Program for Access to Technical Education and Employment (PRONATEC)— all to say “we were able to overcome Meta’s content moderation policies and governance.”

The context surrounding the narrative

Brazil ranks as the world’s second-largest country by WhatsApp users (148 million) and the third-largest addressable Instagram audience (147 million). The country is considered a pioneer in internet governance and digital regulation, with a strong tradition of open, multistakeholder approaches to protecting digital rights, especially thanks to the country's foundational internet law, Federal Law No. 12.965/2014, known as the Marco Civil da Internet.

For more than 10 years, Brazil’s Marco Civil da Internet protected digital platforms from civil liability for third-party content, except when they failed to comply with a specific court order requiring its removal, safeguarding freedom of expression while preventing platforms from being inundated with takedown requests. This changed in June 2025, when the country’s Supreme Court, recognizing shifts in digital media ecosystems, ruled that Federal Law No. 12.965/2014 was partially unconstitutional because it no longer sufficiently protected fundamental rights and democracy. The ruling made digital platforms liable for third parties’ content in Brazil, a decision experts argue is impossible to fulfill until digital platforms offer real transparency into their content moderation policies and governance practices. 

In October 2026, Sleeping Giant Brasil shared a report on what they consider evidence of Meta’s “algorithmic favoritism” toward the Bolsonaros’ political allies, focusing on the case of Nikolas Ferreira, a right-wing politician affiliated with the Liberal Party (PL) — currently serving as a Member of the Chamber of Deputies, elected for a four-year term in 2022.

On October 14, the Brazilian independent news site Nucleo shared an investigation showing how Meta’s AI favored creating images of Flávio Bolsonaro on WhatsApp. According to the outlet, Meta acknowledged the failure via email and said it would take the necessary measures to prevent it from happening again.

On October 15, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) ruled that Meta must refrain from interfering with the distribution of political and electoral content posted by either Lula da Silva or Flávio Bolsonaro until the conclusion of the election’s second round, stating that failure to comply with the ruling would result in a daily fine of BRL 500,000 (USD 91,942). The decision came after Lula da Silva’s reelection campaign team denounced to the TSE that Meta repeatedly restricted the reach of publications linked to the government candidate and his supporters

On October 16, the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that Meta employees acknowledged in internal communications that restrictions during the country's election hindered the Instagram accounts of Lula da Silva.

Meta acknowledged technical issues on its platforms on October 16, but said they were not the result of political bias. In an official statement, the company said the “ad account for Lula’s campaign was deactivated by mistake for just over an hour, and not for political reasons,” and that several of the reported problems were part of a “global” failure. 

In his celebration speech, Lula da Silva promised to prioritize new regulations that ensure big digital media platforms are held accountable. He stated that during the recent election, he and his allies had to “overcome outside interference coming in through digital platforms,” and argued Brazil “cannot have monstrous companies earning billions, paying no taxes, and trying to steer” the country’s elections.

Social media and disinformation have played a central role in past elections in Brazil, as research shared by Harvard Kennedy School’s Misinformation Review, a scholarly publication, argues that in the 2022 election, “susceptibility to electoral misinformation is affected by factors such as political ideology, trust in the electoral process and democratic institutions, and information consumption, with those who participate in political groups in messaging apps being more likely to believe in electoral misinformation.”

As in 2022 but without the coup plot, the Bolsonaro family alleges electoral fraud. In a first letter shared after fleeing the country amid open investigations linking him to money laundering, Flávio Bolsonaro first declared himself “the elected president,” then deleted it and replaced it with a second version calling himself the rightful “leader” of Brazil. Bolsonaro argues in the text that he had to leave the country to prevent political persecution. 

Although Flávio Bolsonaro insisted he would seek to annul the presidential election, his party later distanced itself from that position in a statement and chose to accept the official results, while still reporting irregularities during the electoral process.

Written by Civic Media Observatory, Samanta Azpurua
